Continuous Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving

ISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06
Baran Atalar Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA email: batalar@andrew.cmu.edu , Xutong Liu Affiliation: University of Washington Tacoma, Tacoma, Washington, USA email: xutongl@uw.edu , Jinhang Zuo Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong, China email: jinhang.zuo@cityu.edu.hk , Siwei Wang Affiliation: Microsoft Research Asia, China email: siweiwang@microsoft.com , Wei Chen Affiliation: Microsoft Research Asia, China email: weic@microsoft.com and Carlee Joe-Wong Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA email: cjoewong@andrew.cmu.edu
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly popular, caching responses so that they can be reused by users with semantically similar queries has become a vital strategy for reducing inference costs and latency. Existing caching frameworks have proposed to decide which query responses to cache by assuming a finite, known universe of discrete queries and learning their serving costs and arrival probabilities. As LLMs’ pool of users and queries expands, however, such an assumption becomes increasingly untenable: real-world LLM queries reside in an infinite, continuous embedding space. In this paper, we establish the first rigorous theoretical framework for semantic LLM response caching in continuous query space under uncertainty. To bridge the gap between discrete optimization and continuous representation spaces, we introduce dynamic ϵ\epsilon-net discretization coupled with Kernel Ridge Regression. This design enables the system to formally quantify estimation uncertainty and generalize partial feedback on LLM query costs across continuous semantic query neighborhoods. We develop both offline learning and online adaptive algorithms optimized to reduce switching costs incurred by changing the cached responses. We prove that our online algorithm achieves a sublinear regret bound against an optimal continuous oracle, which reduces to existing bounds for discrete query models. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that our framework approximates the continuous optimal cache well while also reducing computational and switching overhead compared to existing methods.

Keywords: 
Large Language Models, Semantic Caching, Online learning

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have recently exploded in popularity, with ChatGPT reportedly reaching 700 million users in July 2025 (Chatterji et al., 2025). LLM queries, however, are expensive (Samsi et al., 2023): not only can they have seconds-level response latencies, but LLM inference can have significant energy costs and compute utilization, costs that will only grow with query volume. Prior work has suggested caching query responses to reduce these costs: cached responses can then be returned directly for semantically similar queries, eliminating the need for a LLM inference pass. Caching is particularly effective for queries that seek factual, non-user-specific information, which make up a significant portion of ChatGPT usage (Chatterji et al., 2025).

While caching presents a natural solution to reducing LLM inference costs, deciding which queries and responses to cache, which we refer to as the cache design problem, presents a significant research challenge: cache sizes are limited, so the most frequently arriving and/or most expensive query-response pairs should be prioritized for caching. These costs and arrival probabilities are often unknown and stochastic, and thus must be estimated from offline data or online experience. Prior work has addressed such challenges in other caching settings (Paschos et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020), but the LLM setting raises novel challenges. Firstly, we should relate semantically similar queries in order to reduce cache misses, instead of relying on exact query matches like some existing LLM frameworks (Zhu et al., 2023). Indeed, some recent work has found that more than 30% of LLM queries are semantically similar (Gill et al., 2024). Secondly, initial work on semantic caching for LLMs relies on the assumption that query-response caching candidates are drawn from a known, finite list (Bang, 2023; Stogiannidis et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Gill et al., 2024). One can then apply online or offline learning methods to estimate the cost of serving each query, as well as its arrival probability, and choose what to cache accordingly (Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). As LLMs grow more popular and their queries and users more diverse, it becomes almost impossible to enumerate such a finite set of queries and responses.

We address these challenges by considering semantic caching over continuous query space. Learning query costs and arrival probabilities is thus significantly harder: since future queries can come from anywhere in the continuous query space, the cost and arrival probability of each query must be inferred from those of other queries instead of directly estimated from the history of the same query. Even if these parameters can be inferred, we must now optimize over an infinite space of possible query-response cache candidates, potentially introducing significant suboptimality into the cache design. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to propose a semantic caching framework for low-cost LLM serving in continuous query space with theoretical performance guarantees.

1.1. Related Work

Low-Cost LLM Serving. As the deployment of LLM models scales, lowering their high inference costs has become an important research direction. While optimization techniques such as quantization  (Dettmers et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023) and speculative decoding  (Leviathan et al., 2023; Spector and Re, 2023) reduce compute overhead, caching has emerged as a highly effective method to reduce redundant computations entirely. Previous works have investigated caching at multiple levels, from reusing internal KV-states  (Pope et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023; Sheng et al., 2023) to routing API requests  (Qu et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024). At the query level, earlier works relied on exact-text matching  (Zhu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025), which is restrictive for natural language prompts. This limitation led to the development of semantic caching  (Gim et al., 2023; Gill et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024), allowing similar queries to share responses. While recent systems extend semantic caching to richer settings such as multi-turn contexts  (Yan et al., 2025) and tiered architectures  (Singh et al., 2026), they remain fundamentally heuristic based and assume knowledge of query costs or arrival distributions or do not generalize across a continuous query space. Our work tackles the more complex and realistic scenario of caching over an unbounded, continuous query space with uncertain query costs and arrivals.

Learning-Based Cache Optimization. Traditional caching methods, such as LFU (least frequently used) and LRU (least recently used) (Lee et al., 2001), are simple online heuristics that adapt to observed request patterns without explicitly modeling system parameters. In contrast, cost-aware variants such as LEC (Bahn, 2005) estimate quantities like request probabilities and retrieval costs to guide caching decisions. In our previous work (Liu et al., 2026), we introduced an online adaptation framework for semantic caching, but it remained restricted to a finite, discrete query set. Transitioning to a continuous domain inherently changes the mathematical structure of the problem. Specifically, our continuous caching framework can be modeled as a variant of the Combinatorial Multi-Armed Bandit (CMAB) problem (Chen et al., 2013). Unlike standard CMAB settings, our environment introduces a "reverse feedback" challenge: when a query is served from the cache, the true cost of its execution on the LLM remains unobserved.

1.2. Our Contributions

Our work makes the following contributions:

(1) Continuous Semantic Caching Model (Section 2) We model a sequence of queries, each drawn from an a priori unknown probability distribution over the continuous query space, arriving at a LLM operator (Figure 1). Upon arrival, a query is either served from the cache or from the LLM, depending on whether the mismatch cost of serving the cached response of a semantically similar query exceeds the serving cost of LLM inference on this query. To handle infinite query space, we introduce the notion of an ϵ\epsilon-net that partitions the query space into Voronoi regions with semantically similar queries. Given an ϵ\epsilon-net, one can then discretize the cache design problem by caching at most one representative query per region. Importantly, we do not assume a pre-defined ϵ\epsilon-net, as covering the entire query space is likely intractable. We then face the challenge that solely working with these ϵ\epsilon-net query candidates introduces not only discretization errors in choosing the optimal cached queries but also additional errors in estimating query costs, as semantically similar queries may still have distinct serving costs. We address these in our theoretical analysis below.

(2) Algorithm Design: We consider three cache design settings. First, in the oracle setting (Section 3) with full information of query costs and arrivals, we use our ϵ\epsilon-net definition to provide the Reverse Greedy algorithm with provable approximation and discretization guarantees. We then consider the offline setting (Section 4), where historical serving and arrival data is available (e.g., from deployment logs (Zhu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025)). We use this data to build an ϵ\epsilon-net and introduce a pessimistic learning algorithm, CUCB-SC-Cont, that uses kernel ridge regression (KRR) to estimate the serving cost and query arrival probability for a given query from those of other queries in the historical data. Finally, in the online adaptive setting (Section 5), we propose CLCB-SC-LS-Cont, which adaptively constructs an ϵ\epsilon-net on online query arrivals. The online setting further introduces a low-switching constraint not present in traditional CMAB: changing the cache may require re-running some queries to get their responses to cache. We thus design adaptive thresholds that minimize such cache switching along with traditional algorithm regret.

(3) Theoretical Guarantees: After deriving an approximation guarantee for the oracle setting, we provide a suboptimality guarantee for CUCB-SC-Cont in the offline setting. To do so, we introduce a novel method to quantify the KRR estimation error for the model parameters and the resulting cache suboptimality. We then use these results to analyze the optimal choice of ϵ\epsilon, trading off between a lower discretization and estimation errors. Finally, we derive a regret upper bound for CLCB-SC-LS-Cont, despite the continuous space from which our queries are drawn.

(4) Performance Evaluation (Section 6): We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets for offline and online settings. We show that CUCB-SC-Cont achieves the lowest suboptimality gap in the offline setting, yielding up to a 73.32% improvement over prior methods. In the online setting, CLCB-SC-LS-Cont outperforms baselines regarding final average regret, with up to 72.41% and 43.14% reductions observed on synthetic and bursty real-world query streams, respectively. In addition, our algorithm maintains these strong regret results while keeping runtime highly competitive with existing semantic caching baselines.

Due to space constraints, we defer all theoretical proofs and additional experimental results to our extended technical report (Atalar et al., 2026).

2. System Model

In this section, we present the system model of the continuous semantic caching problem for low-cost LLM serving (Fig. 1).

2.1. LLM Serving System

We formalize our LLM serving system as follows.

Queries and Embeddings. We assume queries, which each represent a natural language prompt, are independently drawn from a probability density function f:𝒳→ℝ+f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} over a continuous space 𝒳⊂ℝde\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} such that ∫𝒳f⁡(x)​𝑑x=1\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(x)\,dx=1. We assume that 𝒳\mathcal{X} inherits a metric structure through a distance function d:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ+d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} (e.g., Euclidean distance in the embedding space). We let p≤dep\leq d_{e} denote the intrinsic (metric) dimension of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Specifically, we assume that there exists a constant c0>0c_{0}>0 such that for any x∈𝒳x\in{\mathcal{X}} and any sufficiently small radius r>0r>0, ∫B⁡(x,r)f⁡(x′)​d​x′≥c0​rp\int_{B(x,r)}f(x^{\prime})dx^{\prime}\geq c_{0}r^{p} where B⁡(x,r)={x′∈𝒳:d⁡(x,x′)≤r}.B(x,r)=\{x^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{X}}:d(x,x^{\prime})\leq r\}.

Serving Costs and Partial Observations. Each query x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} is associated with an unknown expected serving cost c⁡(x)∈(0,1]c(x)\in(0,1], representing, for example, latency or computational cost of invoking the LLM. When the system queries the LLM with input xx, it observes a noisy realization Ct​(x)=c⁡(x)+ηt​(x)C_{t}(x)=c(x)+\eta_{t}(x), where the noise sequence ηt​(x)\eta_{t}(x) is conditionally RR-sub-Gaussian given the history ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} (i.e., 𝔼⁡[ηt​(x)|ℱt−1]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t}(x)|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=0 and 𝔼⁡[exp​(ξ​ηt​(x))|ℱt−1]≤exp​(ξ2​R2/2)\mathbb{E}[\text{exp}(\xi\eta_{t}(x))|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq\text{exp}(\xi^{2}R^{2}/2) for all ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R}). This cost is only observed when the LLM is invoked.

Similarity and Mismatch Costs. For a semantic cache of at most kk query-response pairs ℳ={(u1,a⁡(u1)),…,(uk,a⁡(uk))},ui∈𝒳\mathcal{M}=\{(u_{1},a(u_{1})),\ldots,(u_{k},a(u_{k}))\},\quad u_{i}\in\mathcal{X}, we define the distance from a query xx to the cache as d⁡(x,ℳ):=minu∈ℳ⁡d⁡(x,u)d(x,\mathcal{M}):=\min_{u\in\mathcal{M}}d(x,u), and denote the closest cached query by s⁡(x,ℳ):=argminu∈ℳd​(x,u)s(x,\mathcal{M}):=\argmin_{u\in\mathcal{M}}d(x,u). Note that to satisfy the Lipschitz continuity required for our theoretical guarantees, dd must be a well-defined metric space distance (e.g., the Euclidean distance between L2L_{2}-normalized embeddings). If a query xx is served using the cached response corresponding to u∈ℳu\in\mathcal{M}, it incurs an expected mismatch cost ϕ⁡(d⁡(x,u))\phi(d(x,u)), where ϕ:ℝ+→[0,1]\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow[0,1] is a non-decreasing function. Because queries arrive from an infinite continuous space, a user prompt can be significantly different from all previously cached items, potentially yielding an arbitrarily large geometric distance. Bounding the mismatch penalty to a maximum of 11 explicitly caps the cost of these extreme outliers, ensuring the cache penalty never outscales the normalized cost of querying the LLM, while providing the strict upper bounds required for our theoretical regret guarantees. For example, ϕ\phi could be selected as a clipped linear function, ϕ⁡(d)=min⁡(ζ​d,1)\phi(d)=\min(\zeta d,1) for some scaling parameter ζ>0\zeta>0. On the other hand, querying the LLM directly on xx incurs no mismatch cost.

2.2. Semantic Caching

The system maintains a semantic cache ℳ\mathcal{M} defined before. At each round tt, a query x∼fx\sim f arrives. The system chooses between:

  • •

    Cache Lookup: Serve using s⁡(x,ℳ)s(x,\mathcal{M}) and incur mismatch cost ϕ⁡(d⁡(x,ℳ))\phi(d(x,\mathcal{M}));

  • •

    LLM Query: Query the LLM, incur and observe cost c⁡(x)c(x).

The optimal decision rule compares the two costs:

(1) at={LLM​(x)if ​c​(x)≤ϕ⁡(d⁡(x,ℳ)),a⁡(s⁡(x,ℳ))otherwise.\displaystyle a_{t}=\begin{cases}\texttt{LLM}(x)&\text{if }c(x)\leq\phi(d(x,\mathcal{M})),\\ a(s(x,\mathcal{M}))&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

This raises the central question: how should we construct the cache ℳ\mathcal{M} in a continuous query space?

Discretization via ϵ\epsilon-Net and Voronoi Regions. Optimizing directly over the continuous space 𝒳\mathcal{X} is intractable. To obtain a finite representation, we approximate 𝒳\mathcal{X} using an ϵ\epsilon-net 𝒮={x1,…,xm}⊆𝒳\mathcal{S}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}\subseteq\mathcal{X} such that for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, there exists xi∈𝒮x_{i}\in\mathcal{S} with d⁡(x,xi)≤ϵd(x,x_{i})\leq\epsilon.

The set 𝒮\mathcal{S} induces a partition of the space into mm regions {Vi}i=1m\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, defined as Voronoi regions:

Vi:={x∈𝒳:d(x,xi)≤d(x,xj),∀j≠i}.V_{i}:=\{x\in\mathcal{X}:d(x,x_{i})\leq d(x,x_{j}),\;\forall j\neq i\}.

Each region ViV_{i} contains all queries whose closest representative in 𝒮\mathcal{S} is xix_{i}. This induces a finite partition of the continuous query space. We define the weight of each region ViV_{i} as

wi:=∫Vif⁡(x)​𝑑x,w_{i}:=\int_{V_{i}}f(x)\,dx,

i.e., the probability mass of queries in this region.

Loss Function over Continuous Query Space. The expected loss of a cache ℳ\mathcal{M} under density ff is

(2) ℒ⁡(ℳ,f,c,d)=∫𝒳f⁡(x)​min​{c⁡(x),ϕ⁡(d⁡(x,ℳ))}​𝑑x.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M};f,c,d)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(x)\min\{c(x),\phi(d(x,\mathcal{M}))\}dx.

The cache design problem aims to find:

(3) ℳ∗=argminℳ⊆𝒳,|ℳ|≤kℒ​(ℳ,f,c,d)\displaystyle\textstyle\mathcal{M}^{*}=\argmin_{\mathcal{M}\subseteq{\mathcal{X}},|\mathcal{M}|\leq k}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M};f,c,d)

Using the ϵ\epsilon-net approximation, we obtain the discretized loss:

(4) ℒ^​(ℳ,𝒮,𝒘,c)=∑i=1mwi​min​{c⁡(xi),ϕ⁡(d⁡(xi,ℳ))}.\displaystyle\textstyle\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},c)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}\min\{c(x_{i}),\phi(d(x_{i},\mathcal{M}))\}.

In our formal theoretical approach, which we detail in the next sections, we bound the approximation error between Equation 2 and Equation 4, which enables us to derive guarantees on the discretized loss and relate it to the expected loss under density ff.

3. Approximate Solution for Continuous Semantic Caching with Known Parameters

In this section, we study the semantic caching problem under the assumption that the arrival distribution and cost function are known. Our formulation builds on the discrete semantic caching framework of (Liu et al., 2026), which considers a finite query set and derives a discrete reverse-greedy approximation algorithm. However, since our queries are drawn from a continuous space 𝒳⊂ℝde\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}, we replace (Liu et al., 2026)’s finite sum objective with Equation 2’s integral loss function. We first show that the cache design problem for the optimal solution over this continuous space is computationally intractable:

Lemma 3.1 (NP-hardness).

The continuous semantic caching problem shown in Equation 3 is NP-hard.

This lemma shows that our formulation is a strict generalization of the discrete setting. In particular, if 𝒳\mathcal{X} is finite and ff is discrete, we recover the setting in (Liu et al., 2026) exactly. Our problem inherits the NP-hardness but introduces additional complexity due to the infinite decision space induced by continuous query space. To address this challenge, we use Section 2.2’s continuous-to-discrete reduction via an ϵ−\epsilon-net. Next, we bound the resulting discretization error.

Assumption 1 (Lipschitz Continuity of the Expected Cost).

Define gℳ​(x)=min⁡{c⁡(x),ϕ⁡(d⁡(x,ℳ))}∈[0,1]g_{\mathcal{M}}(x)=\min\{c(x),\phi(d(x,\mathcal{M}))\}\in[0,1]. Assume there is a constant Lg>0L_{g}>0 such that for all cache ℳ\mathcal{M}, x→gℳ​(x)x\rightarrow g_{\mathcal{M}}(x) is LgL_{g}-Lipschitz:

|gℳ​(x)−gℳ​(y)|≤Lg​d​(x,y)∀x,y∈𝒳\displaystyle|g_{\mathcal{M}}(x)-g_{\mathcal{M}}(y)|\leq L_{g}d(x,y)\quad\forall x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}

Note that a sufficient condition for Assumption 1 to hold is that both c⁡(x)c(x) and ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) are themselves Lipschitz continuous.

Lemma 3.2 (Continuous-to-discrete approximation via ε\varepsilon-net).

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a static ϵ\epsilon-net covering the space 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} and suppose that Assumption 1 holds. Then for every ℳ\mathcal{M} with |ℳ|≤k|\mathcal{M}|\leq k:

|ℒ⁡(ℳ)−ℒ^​(ℳ,𝒮)|≤Lg​ϵ\displaystyle|\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M})-\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M};\mathcal{S})|\leq L_{g}\epsilon

This lemma shows that the continuous objective can be well approximated by its discrete counterpart. The approximation error scales linearly with the covering radius ϵ\epsilon and with this bound, the problem reduces to a finite optimization problem over 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

We directly apply Lemma 2 from (Liu et al., 2026) to design Algorithm 1. This lemma shows that our discretized loss function is supermodular and non-increasing regarding the set ℳ\mathcal{M}. Theorem 3.3 provides a guarantee on the performance of Alg. 1 following (Il’ev, 2001) and combining this result with Lemma 3.2.

Theorem 3.3 (Approximation Guarantee (Il’ev, 2001)).

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the solution returned by Algorithm 1. Then, ℒ^​(ℳ,𝒮,𝐰,𝐜)≤α⋅ℒ^​(ℳ∗,𝒮,𝐰,𝐜)\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},\bm{c})\leq\alpha\cdot\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M}^{*};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},\bm{c}), where α=eΓ−1Γ,Γ=s1−s\alpha=\frac{e^{\Gamma}-1}{\Gamma},\quad\Gamma=\frac{s}{1-s} and s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1] is the curvature and ℒ⁡(ℳ,𝒮,𝐰,𝐜)−α⋅ℒ⁡(ℳ∗,𝒮,𝐰,𝐜)≤ℒ^​(ℳ,𝒮,𝐰,𝐜)−α⋅ℒ^​(ℳ∗,𝒮,𝐰,𝐜)+(1+α)​Lg​ϵ\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},\bm{c})-\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M}^{*};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},\bm{c})\leq\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},\bm{c})-\alpha\cdot\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M}^{*};\mathcal{S},\bm{w},\bm{c})+(1+\alpha)L_{g}\epsilon.

4. Offline Learning for Continuous Semantic Caching Problem with Unknown Parameters

In this section, we consider the semantic caching problem when the cost function c⁡(x)c(x) and density ff are unknown and must be learned from an offline dataset. Unlike the setting in Section 3, where ff and cc are assumed known, we are given a dataset of observations {(ℳt,xt,Ct)}t=1n\{(\mathcal{M}_{t},x_{t},C_{t})\}_{t=1}^{n}, where CtC_{t} denotes the cost incurred when serving query xtx_{t} and ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} is the selected cache at round tt. If Ct=∅C_{t}=\emptyset, it indicates that the cached response from the nearest neighbor in ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} was used and no cost was observed. If Ct>0C_{t}>0, the LLM was invoked and the cost feedback was recorded.

Our formulation extends the discrete semantic caching framework of (Liu et al., 2026), which assumes a finite query set and estimates costs using empirical means. The key difference from (Liu et al., 2026) is that their framework does not require generalization across inputs. In contrast, our setting requires learning the cost function over a continuous space and making predictions for previously unseen queries. This introduces two key challenges: (i) estimating c⁡(x)c(x) over a continuous domain, and (ii) incorporating estimation uncertainty into the cache optimization problem.

To address these challenges, we model c⁡(x)c(x) using kernel ridge regression (KRR) in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Building on established kernelized bandit frameworks (Chowdhury and Gopalan, 2017), KRR provides both the non-parametric flexibility to learn complex serving cost functions and the closed form posterior variance necessary to construct confidence bounds that enable optimal cache selection.

Since computing the optimal cache is NP-hard even when the parameters are known (Lemma 3.1), we instead aim to learn an approximate solution that competes with the α\alpha-approximate oracle returned by the Continuous Reverse Greedy algorithm (Alg. 1). This algorithm is consistent with prior work on discrete semantic caching (Liu et al., 2026), where the same approximation notion is adopted due to computational intractability. Accordingly, our goal is to minimize the approximate suboptimality defined with respect to this oracle:

(5) SubOpt​(ℳ)=ℒ⁡(ℳ)−α⋅ℒ⁡(ℳ∗),\displaystyle\text{SubOpt}(\mathcal{M})={\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M})-\alpha\cdot{\mathcal{L}}(\mathcal{M}^{*}),

Before proceeding with the CUCB-SC-Cont algorithm (shown in Algorithm 2), we provide the following definitions. For a query xx, we define the kernel vector κx=[κ⁡(xt1,x),…,κ⁡(xtℓ,x)]⊤\kappa_{x}=[\kappa(x_{t_{1}},x),\dots,\kappa(x_{t_{\ell}},x)]^{\top}, where {(xti,Cti)}i=1ℓ\{(x_{t_{i}},C_{t_{i}})\}_{i=1}^{\ell} are the subset of queries for which the LLM was invoked and the cost was observed and {t1,…,tℓ}⊆{1,…,n}\{t_{1},...,t_{\ell}\}\subseteq\{1,...,n\} are the indices where the LLM was actually queried. Note that κ⁡(x,x)\kappa(x,x) is a scalar measuring self-similarity, whereas κx\kappa_{x} is a vector of similarities between xx and the observed data. We define the kernel (Gram) matrix K∈ℝℓ×ℓK\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell\times\ell} as Ki​j=κ⁡(xti,xtj),K_{ij}=\kappa(x_{t_{i}},x_{t_{j}}), ∀i,j∈[ℓ]\forall i,j\in[\ell] and the vector of observed costs as y=[Ct1,…,Ctℓ]⊤y=[C_{t_{1}},...,C_{t_{\ell}}]^{\top}.

Algorithm 2 presents our offline learning procedure for the continuous semantic caching problem with unknown parameters. The algorithm first constructs an ϵ\epsilon-net 𝒮\mathcal{S} over the observed embeddings (Line 2), which serves as a finite discretization of the continuous space. Each point in 𝒮\mathcal{S} represents a local region, and we estimate its arrival weight w^i\hat{w}_{i} by computing the empirical fraction of queries that fall into its corresponding cell (i.e., region) (Line 3). To learn the unknown serving cost function c⁡(x)c(x), we apply kernel KRR using only the subset of queries for which the LLM was actually invoked (non-empty cost values), yielding an estimate c^​(x)\hat{c}(x) along with an uncertainty term σℓ,λ​(x)\sigma_{\ell,\lambda}(x) (Line 4). Based on this, we construct a confidence radius Δ⁡(x)\Delta(x) and define pessimistic cost estimates c¯​(x)\bar{c}(x), which upper bound the true cost with high probability (Line 5). Finally, we apply the reverse greedy oracle on (ℳ,𝒮,𝒘^,𝒄¯)(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{S},\hat{\bm{w}},\bar{\bm{c}}) to compute an approximate optimal cache (Lines 6-7). We directly estimate 𝒘\bm{w} using empirical frequencies in the ϵ−\epsilon-net because every incoming query is observed. In contrast, cost feedback is sparse and recorded only when the LLM is invoked, which necessitates using KRR to generalize across the continuous space. We now present its performance guarantee:

Theorem 4.1 (Suboptimality Gap Bound for Algorithm 2).

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be an offline dataset of n≥8​log⁡(m/δ)mini⁡wi​νin\geq\frac{8\log(m/\delta)}{\min_{i}w_{i}\nu_{i}} samples. Then with probability of at least 1−δ1-\delta, the cache ℳ^\hat{\mathcal{M}} returned by CUCB-SC-Cont satisfies the following where ℓk\ell_{k} is the parameter of the RBF kernel, Cν>0C_{\nu}>0 is a constant and νi\nu_{i} is the query propensity of cell ii (the probability that we observe the cost of an arriving query in cell ii):

SubOpt​(ℳ^)≤(α+1)​(2​m​ln⁡(2/δ)n⏟Arrival+Lg​2​dem1/de⏟Discretization)\displaystyle\text{SubOpt}(\hat{\mathcal{M}})\leq(\alpha+1)\Bigg(\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{2m\ln(2/\delta)}{n}}}_{\text{Arrival}}+\underbrace{L_{g}\frac{2\sqrt{d_{e}}}{m^{1/d_{e}}}}_{\text{Discretization}}\Bigg)
+4​α​(B+log⁡(2​m/δ)2​ℓ​λ)​2​de​(∑iνi−1)1/pℓk​Cν​m1/de​(2​log⁡(1/δ)n)1/p⏟Cost.\displaystyle\quad+\;\underbrace{4\alpha\left(B+\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2\ell\lambda}}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt{d_{e}}\left(\sum_{i}\nu_{i}^{-1}\right)^{1/p}}{\ell_{k}C_{\nu}m^{1/d_{e}}}\left(\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{n}\right)^{1/p}}}_{\text{Cost}}.

While the covering number mm scales exponentially with the embedding dimension ded_{e}, creating a potential bottleneck, we explicitly manage this dependency in Remark 2 in our technical report (Atalar et al., 2026) by deriving an optimal discretization radius ϵ∗\epsilon^{*} that balances mm against the sample size nn to ensure the suboptimality gap converges to 0.

Our proposed algorithm and analysis can be viewed as a continuous analogue of the offline CUCB-SC algorithm in (Liu et al., 2026), but introduce several key differences that also drive our technical contributions. Unlike the discrete setting, we do not assume a known finite query universe and instead approximate the arrival distribution via an ϵ\epsilon-net over the embedding space, incurring a discretization error absent in the discrete case. Moreover, rather than estimating costs independently per query, we learn a continuous cost function c⁡(x)c(x) using KRR, leading to confidence bounds for each candidate query that depend on the number of observed cost samples ℓ\ell rather than the total number of queries nn. These differences require jointly addressing geometric approximation and nonparametric function estimation, yielding three main contributions: (i) quantifying the discretization error induced by the ϵ\epsilon-net, (ii) replacing per-query empirical estimates with KRR-based cost learning and uncertainty quantification, and (iii) deriving geometry-aware bounds on the KRR posterior width by linking local sample counts within Voronoi cells to nearest-neighbor radii and RKHS distances under the RBF kernel. Together, these elements translate continuous-space uncertainty into a suboptimality bound that decomposes into arrival-estimation, cost-estimation, and discretization errors.

The bound in Theorem 4.1 decomposes into three terms corresponding to distinct sources of error in the continuous semantic caching setting. (i) Arrival estimation error: The term 𝒪⁡(mn)\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}\right) arises from estimating the arrival weights 𝒘\bm{w} from nn samples, and matches the concentration rate in the discrete setting (Liu et al., 2026). (ii) Cost estimation error: Reflects the difficulty of learning a continuous cost function c⁡(x)c(x) from partial observations. Unlike the discrete case, where the estimation error scales as 𝒪(n−1/2)\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2}), the continuous setting incurs a slower rate 𝒪(n−1/(2p))\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/(2p)}) due to the nonparametric nature of the problem and the need to generalize across nearby queries. This term captures the interaction between kernel smoothness (through ℓk\ell_{k}), intrinsic dimension pp, and the local observation propensities νi\nu_{i}. (iii) Discretization error: The term 𝒪(m−1/de)\mathcal{O}\!\left(m^{-1/d_{e}}\right) arises from approximating the continuous space 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} using an ϵ\epsilon-net of size mm, and vanishes as the discretization becomes finer. This term has no analogue in the discrete setting, where the query space is finite and known.

Comparison to the Discrete Case and Reduction. In the discrete setting (Liu et al., 2025), the suboptimality gap scales as 𝒪⁡(∑qν​(q)−1n),\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{q}\nu(q)^{-1}}{n}}\right), reflecting finite-arm estimation with no geometric structure. In contrast, our bound generalizes this result to continuous spaces by introducing both geometric approximation and functional estimation terms. Specifically, while the dependence on νi\nu_{i} is preserved, it is attenuated through the dimension-dependent exponent 1/(2​p)1/(2p), and the rate in nn degrades from n−1/2n^{-1/2} to n−1/(2p)n^{-1/(2p)} due to the nonparametric nature of learning the continuous cost function. Additionally, new dependencies on the kernel parameter ℓk\ell_{k} and discretization level mm arise. At the same time, our result recovers the discrete case as a special instance. When the query space is finite and coincides with the ϵ\epsilon-net (i.e., ϵ=0\epsilon=0 and m=|𝒬|m=|{\mathcal{Q}}|), and when the kernel does not induce smoothing across distinct queries, the geometric and discretization terms vanish. In this regime, cost estimation reduces to per-query empirical estimation, and the bound recovers the same qualitative 𝒪(n−1/2)\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2}) scaling as in the discrete CUCB-SC analysis. This demonstrates that our result is a strict generalization of the discrete setting.

Proof Sketch. The full proof may be found in (Atalar et al., 2026). To establish the result in Theorem 4.1, we use the following lemma with the concentration bound guarantees.

Lemma 4.2 (Concentration of Estimates).

For any δ>0\delta>0, define the following events: ℰarvl≔{∥𝐰^−𝐰∥1≤2​m​ln⁡(2/δ)n},ℰcost≔{|c¯(x)−c(x)|≤22(B+log⁡(2​m/δ)2​ℓ​λ)min{1,2​ϵℓk(2​log⁡(1/δ)n​wi​νi​νi¯)1/p}∀x∈𝒮},ℰcounter≔{Ni≥n⋅wi​νi2,∀i∈[m]}\mathcal{E}_{\text{arvl}}\coloneqq\Big\{\|\hat{\bm{w}}-\bm{w}\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{2m\ln(2/\delta)}{n}}\Big\},\quad\mathcal{E}_{\text{cost}}\coloneqq\bigg\{|\bar{c}(x)-c(x)|\leq 2\sqrt{2}\left(B+\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2\ell\lambda}}\right)\min\biggl\{1,\frac{2\epsilon}{\ell_{k}}\left(\frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{nw_{i}\nu_{i}\underline{\nu_{i}}}\right)^{1/p}\biggr\}\forall x\in\mathcal{S}\bigg\},\mathcal{E}_{\text{counter}}\coloneqq\Big\{N_{i}\geq\frac{n\cdot w_{i}\nu_{i}}{2},\;\forall i\in[m]\Big\} where NiN_{i} is the number of observed cost samples in cell ViV_{i}, νi¯>0\underline{\nu_{i}}>0 is a constant and ℓk\ell_{k} is the kernel parameter, c∈ℋkc\in\mathcal{H}_{k} (RKHS) with ‖c‖ℋk≤B\|c\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\leq B. Then, assuming n≥8​log⁡(m/δ)mini⁡wi​νin\geq\frac{8\log(m/\delta)}{\min_{i}w_{i}\nu_{i}}, all three events occur with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Lemma 4.2 characterizes a high-probability event under which both arrival weights and costs are accurately estimated. While ℰarvl\mathcal{E}_{\text{arvl}} and ℰcounter\mathcal{E}_{\text{counter}} follow from standard concentration arguments, the event ℰcost\mathcal{E}_{\text{cost}} captures the main technical challenge in the continuous setting. It combines kernel ridge regression confidence with geometric control of the posterior variance, where Lemma A.1 bounds the local sample density via nearest-neighbor radius and Lemma A.2 converts this into a bound on the KRR uncertainty. This yields an explicit cost estimation error that depends on the intrinsic dimension, kernel bandwidth, and local observation probabilities.

Generality of the Kernel Choice. We derive our geometric bounds (Lemma A.2) using the RBF kernel because it is one of the standard choices for continuous embedding spaces. However, our mathematical framework easily extends to other kernels. The idea of bounding the model’s uncertainty based on the distance to the nearest observed neighbor applies to any distance-based kernel, such as the Matérn or Laplacian kernels. Specifically, adapting our proof to these alternatives simply requires updating the specific distance to error formula in Lemma A.2.

Optimal ϵ\epsilon Value. We derive the optimal covering radius ϵ∗\epsilon^{*} in Remark 2, defined as the specific radius that minimizes the algorithm’s proved suboptimality gap in Theorem 4.1. We use the fact that m=𝒪⁡(ϵ−de)m=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-d_{e}}) in this derivation. Our analysis shows that this optimal radius shifts based on the total number of samples nn, embedding dimension ded_{e} and the intrinsic dimension pp. As we collect more data (nn increases), we can shrink ϵ∗\epsilon^{*} to create a finer discretization. However, the geometry of the space also introduces some dependencies: if ded_{e} is large, this requires us to use a corresponding large radius to cover the space. Similarly, if the queries are highly varied rather than tightly clustered (pp increases), the data becomes sparser, again requiring a larger radius. When the embedding dimension is greater than the intrinsic dimension (de≫p)(d_{e}\gg p), the local cost estimation becomes the primary bottleneck and ϵ∗=𝒪⁡(n−12​de+p)\epsilon^{*}=\mathcal{O}\left(n^{-\frac{1}{2d_{e}+p}}\right) becomes the optimal radius.

5. Online Adaptive Learning for the Continuous Semantic Caching Problem

Having developed an offline learning algorithm for the continuous semantic caching problem, we now turn to the online setting, where the system must learn the optimal cache dynamically from a stream of queries without access to a pre-collected dataset. Queries arrive sequentially, drawn from a continuous embedding space, and the algorithm must simultaneously estimate the arrival distribution and the cost function while making caching decisions in real time. We thus face the challenge of partial feedback: the serving cost is observed only when the LLM is queried. The goal is to adaptively update the cache to minimize long-term serving and mismatch cost while balancing exploration (querying the LLM to improve estimates) and exploitation (serving from the cache using current knowledge). To achieve this, we develop two distinct algorithms. Our primary method, which we introduce in this section, dynamically constructs and expands a representative set of queries on the fly to continuously adapt to new semantic regions. In contrast, we also introduce an alternative algorithm in the technical report (Atalar et al., 2026), CLCB-Frozen-Cont, which restricts learning to a fixed frozen candidate pool over stable, discrete stages to provide stricter control over cache updates. Next, we introduce the online learning setup, present the proposed algorithm CLCB-SC-LS-Cont in Algorithm 3, and finally provide theoretical guarantees and analysis.

5.1. Online Learning Setup

We consider a TT-round sequential decision-making problem over a continuous embedding space 𝒳⊂ℝde\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}. At the beginning of each round t∈[T]t\in[T], the system maintains a semantic cache ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} of size kk and a user with query xt∈𝒳x_{t}\in{\mathcal{X}} arrives. As described in Section 2.2, the agent either serves the cached response of the nearest neighbor or queries the LLM for a fresh response and observes the cost.

At the end of round tt, the agent decides whether to update the cache. If ℳt≠ℳt−1\mathcal{M}_{t}\neq\mathcal{M}_{t-1}, the agent incurs a switching cost for fetching and storing the updated queries in ℳt∖ℳt−1\mathcal{M}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{M}_{t-1}.

Learning Objective. The objective is to minimize the cumulative regret relative to the best fixed α\alpha-approximate cache over the time horizon, while accounting for both serving and switching costs. We define our comparator as ℳ𝒩T∗\mathcal{M}^{*}_{\mathcal{N}_{T}}, the optimal cache of size kk selected from the set of all observed queries 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T}. This definition is necessary because, in a practical serving system, we can only populate the cache with query-response pairs that we have actually observed. Formally, letting ℳ0=∅\mathcal{M}_{0}=\emptyset, the expected cumulative regret with switching costs is defined as:

Reg​(T)\displaystyle\textstyle\text{Reg}(T) =𝔼⁡[∑t=1T[ℒ⁡(ℳt)−α​ℒ​(ℳ𝒩T∗)]+∑x∈ℳt∖ℳt−1c⁡(x)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}[\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M}_{t})-\alpha\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M}^{*}_{\mathcal{N}_{T}})]+\sum_{x\in\mathcal{M}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{M}_{t-1}}c(x)\right]

where the expectation is taken over the randomness of the continuous query arrivals, the serving costs, and the cache selection.

5.2. Algorithm Design of CLCB-SC-LS-Cont

In this section, we present CLCB-SC-LS-Cont, an online learning algorithm designed for semantic caching over continuous spaces with low switching costs. The pseudocode is provided in Algorithm 3, with subroutines Switch Cache Continuous in Algorithm 4 and Serve and Update Continuous in Algorithm 5. CLCB-SC-LS-Cont proceeds in four main phases: (i) dynamically constructing a representative discrete state space from prior arrivals, (ii) determining when to switch the cache by defining observation thresholds, (iii) actively exploring unknown serving costs using KRR, and (iv) serving queries while refining the kernel dataset.

Dynamic Representative Set Construction (Algorithm 3, Lines 5-11). As each query xt∼f⁡(x)x_{t}\sim f(x) arrives, the algorithm builds an empirical representative set 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} on the fly. If xtx_{t} is further than the covering radius ϵ\epsilon from all existing centers in 𝒮t−1\mathcal{S}_{t-1}, it is added as a new center (𝒮t=𝒮t−1∪{xt})(\mathcal{S}_{t}=\mathcal{S}_{t-1}\cup\{x_{t}\}), its counters are initialized, and a cache switched is forced to account for this new region of the space. Otherwise, xtx_{t} is mapped to its nearest existing center utu_{t}, and the representative set remains unchanged.

Stage-Based Cache Switching (Algorithm 3, Lines 12-18). To control switching frequency while ensuring sufficient exploration over the expanding set 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t}, we utilize a stage-based switching mechanism. For each center u∈𝒮tu\in\mathcal{S}_{t}, we maintain a local stage index τu\tau_{u}. A new stage is triggered and the Switch flag is set to true, when the number of mapped to uu in the current stage exceeds 1+Tmt​∑τ<τu|𝒯⁡(u,τ)|1+\sqrt{\frac{T}{m_{t}}\sum_{\tau<\tau_{u}}|{\mathcal{T}}(u,\tau)|}. Crucially, this threshold dynamically adjusts based on the current number of active centers mt=|𝒮t|.m_{t}=|\mathcal{S}_{t}|. A similar global stage threshold τf\tau_{f} is maintained to track the arrivals in the current stage.

Active Exploration via KRR Optimism (Algorithm 4, Lines 3-18). When a switch is triggered, the agent must estimate the unknown serving costs to rebuild the cache. To efficiently explore the continuous cost space, we apply the principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty using KRR. For each center u∈𝒮tu\in\mathcal{S}_{t}, the algorithm evaluates the Gram matrix Kt−1K_{t-1} over the exact historically observed query-cost pairs Ot−1O_{t-1}. It computes the KRR posterior mean c^t−1\hat{c}_{t-1} and subtracts a confidence radius Δt−1\Delta_{t-1} which scales with the posterior standard deviation σt−1,λ\sigma_{t-1,\lambda} to obtain the optimistic lower confidence bound c¯t−1\underline{c}_{t-1} (Lines 8-11). The algorithm then calls the Cont_Reverse_Greedy oracle using these optimistic costs and empirical weights w^t−1\hat{w}_{t-1} to construct the new cache ℳ^t\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{t} and queries the LLM to store the responses not existent in the previous cache ℳ^t−1\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{t-1} (Lines 17-18).

Serving and Updating (Algorithm 5, Lines 6-15). After the cache is determined, the agent routes the incoming query xtx_{t} (mapped to center utu_{t}). It compares the optimistic cost of querying the LLM c¯t−1​(ut)\underline{c}_{t-1}(u_{t}), against the mismatch cost ϕ⁡(d⁡(xt,ℳ^))\phi(d(x_{t},\hat{\mathcal{M}})) of serving the query from the cache (Line 6). If c¯t−1​(ut)<ϕ⁡(d⁡(xt,ℳ^t))\underline{c}_{t-1}(u_{t})<\phi(d(x_{t},\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{t})), the agent queries the LLM and observes the exact realized cost Ct​(xt)C_{t}(x_{t}) and appends the tuple (xt,Ct​(xt))(x_{t},C_{t}(x_{t})) to the observation set OtO_{t} (Lines 7-10). This LCB based routing ensures the algorithm actively collects cost feedback in uncertain regions of the continuous space. Otherwise, it serves the user from the cache without incurring LLM costs or updating the KRR dataset (Lines 12-14).

Novelty Compared to the Discrete Case. While CLCB-SC-LS-Cont shares the high-level exploration-exploitation and low-switching logic of its discrete counterpart (Liu et al., 2026), it introduces fundamental algorithmic changes to handle continuous domains. First, rather than operating over a fixed finite set of mm queries, it dynamically constructs an expanding ϵ−\epsilon-net (𝒮t)(\mathcal{S}_{t}), smoothly adapting its stage-switching thresholds to the growing dimension mtm_{t}. Second, while the discrete algorithm relies on independent empirical means to estimate costs, our algorithm leverages KRR to share information across the space. By utilizing a kernel κ⁡(⋅,⋅)\kappa(\cdot,\cdot), the observation of a cost at xtx_{t} reduces the uncertainty σt,λ​(u)\sigma_{t,\lambda}(u) for all nearby centers u,u, thus generalizing the feedback to unobserved regions. Finally, the optimistic confidence intervals transition from standard Hoeffding/Chernoff bounds based strictly on local hit counts to posterior variance, similarly to Theorem 4.1 in the offline case.

5.3. Theoretical Results for CLCB-SC-LS-Cont

In this section, we present our assumption and the main theoretical result characterizing the performance of CLCB-SC-LS-Cont.

Assumption 2 (Cluster-Based Arrival Distribution).

We assume the continuous query arrival distribution f⁡(x)f(x) is highly concentrated, such that the queries naturally cluster around a finite set of optimal semantic cache points ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{*}. Specifically, the maximum distance between any query generated near an optimal cache point and its nearest center in 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} decays as εt=𝒪⁡(1/t)\varepsilon_{t}=\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{t}), while the total number of active ϵ\epsilon-net centers required to cover the high-probability regions of f⁡(x)f(x) remains bounded by a constant meffm_{\text{eff}}.

Justification of Assumption 2. In a worst-case uniform continuous space, achieving a sublinear discretization error would require an ϵ\epsilon-net of size mmax≈𝒪⁡(Tde/2)m_{\max}\approx\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{e}/2}). This exponentially large number of centers would blow up the estimation regret, leading to a rate of 𝒪⁡(Tde+1de+2)\mathcal{O}(T^{\frac{d_{e}+1}{d_{e}+2}}). However, Assumption 2 relies on the practical reality that real-world user queries do not spread out evenly or randomly; instead, they naturally group together around common themes and popular subjects. We empirically validate this behavior in our experimental datasets: as shown in the PCA projection of our synthetic stream (Figure 3 in the technical report (Atalar et al., 2026)) and the UMAP visualization of the combined Natural Questions and TriviaQA datasets (Figure 4 in the technical report (Atalar et al., 2026)), incoming queries strictly concentrate into dense, distinct semantic regions rather than filling the continuous embedding space uniformly. Because of this clustering, the algorithm forms centers within these dense regions. Therefore, the effective number of generated centers, meffm_{\text{eff}}, remains bounded by the geometry of the clusters, and is smaller than the theoretical maximum (meff≤mmaxm_{\text{eff}}\leq m_{\max}).

Theorem 5.1 (Regret of CLCB-SC-LS-Cont).

Let 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T} be the set of all unique queries observed up to horizon TT, and let ℳ𝒩T∗\mathcal{M}^{*}_{\mathcal{N}_{T}} be the optimal cache of size kk selected from 𝒩T\mathcal{N}_{T}. Under Assumption 2, and setting the failure probability to δ=1/T\delta=1/T, the cumulative regret of the CLCB-SC-LS-Cont algorithm is upper bounded by:

Reg​(T)\displaystyle\text{Reg}(T) ≤𝒪⁡(βT​T​γT⏟Cost+meff​T​log⁡T⏟Arrival)\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}\Bigg(\underbrace{\beta_{T}\sqrt{T\gamma_{T}}}_{\text{Cost}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{m_{\text{eff}}T\log T}}_{\text{Arrival}}\Bigg)
+𝒪⁡((1+2​α)​Lg​T⏟Discretization+k​mmax​log⁡log​T⏟Switching )\displaystyle\quad+\mathcal{O}\Bigg(\underbrace{(1+2\alpha)L_{g}\sqrt{T}}_{\text{Discretization}}+\underbrace{km_{\text{max}}\log\log T}_{\text{Switching }}\Bigg)

which achieves a strictly sublinear regret of 𝒪~​(T)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}). βT\beta_{T} is the KRR confidence multiplier, γT\gamma_{T} is the maximum information gain, and α\alpha is the approximation ratio of the Reverse Greedy oracle.

Comparison to the Discrete Regret Bound. Theorem 5.1 establishes that CLCB-SC-LS-Cont achieves a sublinear regret of 𝒪~​(T)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T}) in the continuous domain. This result is nontrivial when compared to the discrete semantic caching bound of 𝒪⁡(m​T​log⁡(m​T)​log⁡log​T)\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{mT\log(mT)}\log\log T\right) derived by (Liu et al., 2026). In the discrete setting, the regret scales with the known, finite number of unique queries mm. However, in our continuous setting, the query space is infinite. We replace the dependence on mm with two continuous analogues: the maximum RKHS information gain γT\gamma_{T}, and the effective covering number me​f​fm_{eff} of the arrival clusters. While the discrete algorithm (Liu et al., 2026) relies on independent arm estimation, our bound isolates the discretization penalty 𝒪⁡(Lg​T)\mathcal{O}(L_{g}\sqrt{T}) from the generalization capability of the KRR model, matching the T\sqrt{T} time-scaling of (Liu et al., 2026) despite operating in an infinite-dimensional action space.

Proof Sketch. The full proof may be found in (Atalar et al., 2026). To prove the main theorem, we establish the following lemmas, which overcome specific technical challenges in the continuous domain.

The following confidence bound for the cost relies on the result established in (Chowdhury and Gopalan, 2017). For any t≥1t\geq 1 and regularization λ>0\lambda>0, let c^t(x)=κt(x)⊤(Kt+λI)−1y1:t\hat{c}_{t}(x)=\kappa_{t}(x)^{\top}(K_{t}+\lambda I)^{-1}y_{1:t} and σt,λ2​(x)=κ⁡(x,x)−κt​(x)⊤​(Kt+λ​I)−1​κt​(x)\sigma_{t,\lambda}^{2}(x)=\kappa(x,x)-\kappa_{t}(x)^{\top}(K_{t}+\lambda I)^{-1}\kappa_{t}(x) denote the standard KRR posterior mean and variance, respectively. We define the information gain as γt=12​log​det(I+1λ​Kt)\gamma_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\log\det(I+\frac{1}{\lambda}K_{t}).

Lemma 5.2 (Any-time concentration of cost and probability estimates).

Assume the true cost c∈ℋkc\in\mathcal{H}_{k} with ‖c‖ℋk≤B\|c\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k}}\leq B, and the noise sequence is conditionally RR-sub-Gaussian. Let meffm_{\text{eff}} be the effective covering number of 𝒳\mathcal{X} at radius ϵ\epsilon. For any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) and horizon T≥1T\geq 1, define the confidence radius βt​(x)=(B+R​2​(γt+ln⁡(2/δ)))​σt,λ​(x)\beta_{t}(x)=\left(B+R\sqrt{2(\gamma_{t}+\ln(2/\delta))}\right)\sigma_{t,\lambda}(x). The joint event ℰ=ℰarr∩ℰcost\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{arr}}\cap\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cost}} holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, where for all t∈[T]t\in[T] and x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}:

ℰarr\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{arr}} ≔{∥𝒘^t−𝒘∥1≤2​meff​ln⁡(2​T2/δ)t},\displaystyle\coloneqq\left\{\|\hat{\bm{w}}_{t}-\bm{w}\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{2m_{\text{eff}}\ln(2T^{2}/\delta)}{t}}\right\},
ℰcost\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cost}} ≔{|c^t−1(x)−c(x)|≤βt−1(x)}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\left\{|\hat{c}_{t-1}(x)-c(x)|\leq\beta_{t-1}(x)\right\}.

Consequently, the lower confidence bound c¯t​(x)=c^t​(x)−βt​(x)\underline{c}_{t}(x)=\hat{c}_{t}(x)-\beta_{t}(x) satisfies c¯t​(x)≤c​(x)\underline{c}_{t}(x)\leq c(x) with high probability.

Lemma 5.2 highlights a fundamental departure from discrete caching. It allows us to construct valid, any-time optimistic lower bounds c¯\underline{c} that generalize across the continuous space based on kernel similarity, forming the basis of our active exploration strategy. We also use Lemma 6 from (Liu et al., 2026) in the proof of Theorem 5.1, which bounds the sensitivity of the loss under optimistic cost estimates, as Lemma 5.2 establishes the anytime LCB of c¯t\underline{c}_{t}.

Lemma 5.3 (Number of cache switches).

Let mmaxm_{\max} be the maximum covering number of the compact query space 𝒳\mathcal{X} at radius ϵ\epsilon, such that mmax≤(D​de/ϵ)dem_{\max}\leq(D\sqrt{d_{e}}/\epsilon)^{d_{e}}, where DD is the diameter in the embedding space. The total number of cache switches triggered by the CLCB-SC-LS-Cont algorithm up to horizon TT is bounded by:

𝔼⁡[∑u∈STτu​(T)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{u\in S_{T}}\tau_{u}(T)\right] ≤𝒪⁡(mmax​log⁡log⁡T),\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}(m_{\max}\log\log T),
𝔼​[τf​(T)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tau_{f}(T)] ≤𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡T).\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}(\log\log T).

Finally, Lemma 5.3 shows how our algorithm avoids excessive cache updates, even as new query clusters are discovered on the fly. In a continuous space, we cannot rely on a fixed set of update rules because the cluster centers are generated dynamically as queries arrive. To solve this, we tie the cache update thresholds to the geometric limits of the space, i.e., the max covering number mmaxm_{\text{max}}.

6. Experiments

In this section, we present the experiments for our Alg. 2 and 3. Additional results including ablations may be found in (Atalar et al., 2026).

Experimental Setup. We consider two types of query universes. The first is a synthetic benchmark consisting of a fixed collection of natural-language prompts (m=50)(m=50) spanning diverse domains and a broad range of prompt lengths, from short keyword-like requests to long conversational questions (similar to the dataset used in (Liu et al., 2026) with prompts that are more varied in their token length) with added Gaussian noise to the embeddings of the sampled prompts to better simulate a continuous query space. The second is a real-data benchmark we formed by combining 2,500 queries from Natural Questions (NQ) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) and 2,500 queries from TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) datasets into a single universe of 5,000 real queries. In both settings, query embeddings xx are obtained using sentence-transformer models (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) that map queries to a 384-dimensional (de)(d_{e}) vector representation, and semantic similarity dd is measured using Euclidean distance after normalization of embeddings, with distances further normalized to lie in 00 to 1.1. Serving costs are derived from GPT-2 tokenizer lengths. For both benchmarks, the expected serving cost c⁡(x)c(x) is the min-max normalized token length of each query xx.

We consider a diverse arrival process across synthetic and real-world datasets. In the synthetic setting, arrivals are generated by first uniformly sampling a query from the discrete query universe and then perturbing its embedding with Gaussian noise. This produces semantically nearby but non-identical arrivals and allows the benchmark to model a continuous query space rather than a purely discrete one. In contrast, in the NQ+TriviaQA setting, each arrival is drawn directly from the pool of real dataset queries, so the stream consists of actual queries from NQ and TriviaQA rather than synthetically perturbed embeddings. To make the real data stream more challenging, the sampling process is bursty and non-uniform where bursts alternate between the two datasets, and within each dataset, queries are sampled from a heavy-tailed popularity distribution governed by a log-normal distribution (details in (Atalar et al., 2026)).

Offline Setting. In the offline setting, we evaluate Algorithm 2 on the synthetic dataset for two ablations using cache size k=5k=5: an ϵ\epsilon ablation for a fixed stream length of t=1000t=1000, and a stream length ablation where ϵ\epsilon is fixed at 0.4 (Figure 2 (a)-(b)). Results are averaged across 20 different seeds for both ablations. We compare against CUCB-SC (Liu et al., 2026), Greedy, Epsilon-Greedy, and LFU (Lee et al., 2001). Greedy selects the cache using the empirical frequency-cost score as Epsilon-Greedy but always exploits, whereas LFU ignores cost entirely and caches only the most frequently observed queries. In the ϵ−\epsilon-ablation, CUCB-SC-Cont achieves the lowest suboptimality gap for small and moderate ϵ\epsilon, but degrades when ϵ\epsilon becomes too large and the discretization becomes too coarse, showing the value of tuning this parameter. CUCB-SC-Cont displays a 52.95% improvement in suboptimality gap over CUCB-SC when ϵ=0.4\epsilon=0.4. In the stream length ablation, CUCB-SC-Cont remains the strongest method overall, while CUCB-SC improves steadily with more offline data and eventually becomes competitive, the other baselines do not show consistent improvement with the increase in stream length. CUCB-SC-Cont achieves significantly better performance than the other baselines when the stream length is small, showing the benefit of generalization via ϵ−\epsilon-net construction and KRR (73.32% improvement over CUCB-SC when stream length OPEN=100)=100).

Online Setting. In the online setting, the CLCB-SC-LS-Cont algorithm demonstrates superior performance in minimizing average regret across both synthetic and real datasets. For the synthetic online dataset, CLCB-SC-LS-Cont achieves the lowest final average regret at 0.0083, which is a 72.41% decrease compared to the most competitive baseline, CLCB-SC-LS (Liu et al., 2026), with a runtime increase of 47.8%. Figure 2 (c) illustrates that while traditional baselines like LFU (Lee et al., 2001) and Epsilon-Greedy exhibit much higher regret peaks and slower convergence, the CLCB-SC-LS-Cont variant converges rapidly. On the combined NQ + TriviaQA dataset, the algorithm maintains this advantage with a final average regret of 0.0061, representing a 63.27% reduction over Greedy. While Figure 2 (f) shows a more significant runtime trade-off for the real combined dataset, the algorithm still outperforms the CLCB-SC-LS baseline by 43.14% in regret while maintaining a nearly identical latency of approximately 250 seconds. The increase in runtime when comparing plots (d) and (f) stems from the fact that for the real dataset, the CLCB-SC-LS-Cont and CLCB-SC-LS trigger more frequent switches.

7. Conclusion

In this paper, we established the first theoretical framework for semantic caching in a continuous query space under uncertainty for low-cost LLM serving. By introducing ϵ−\epsilon-net discretization and KRR, we studied the caching problem across oracle, offline and online settings. Our theoretical analysis establishes suboptimality and sublinear regret guarantees, coupled with empirical evaluations demonstrating significant reduction in regret. Future work includes establishing lower bounds on the semantic LLM caching problem and finer characterization of realistic query distributions, which we can use to improve our caching strategies.

Here we provide the missing proofs in the main body for the presented algorithms as well as additional empirical results. We also introduce our Frozen algorithm and its corresponding proofs and empirical results.

A.1. Proofs for CUCB-SC-Cont and CLCB-SC-LS-Cont

Proof of Lemma 3.1.

We prove NP-hardness by reduction from the discrete semantic caching problem studied in (Liu et al., 2026), which is NP-hard. Consider an arbitrary instance of the discrete problem with a finite query set Q={q1,…,qn}⊂𝒳,Q=\{q_{1},\dots,q_{n}\}\subset\mathcal{X}, query probabilities p⁡(q)p(q), recomputation costs c⁡(q)c(q), and mismatch penalty ϕ⁡(d⁡(q,M))\phi(d(q,M)). Construct an instance of the continuous problem by defining the arrival distribution ff as a discrete measure supported on QQ: f⁡(x)=∑q∈Qp⁡(q)​δ​(x−q),f(x)=\sum_{q\in Q}p(q)\,\delta(x-q), where δ⁡(⋅)\delta(\cdot) denotes the Dirac delta function.

Substituting this choice of ff into the continuous loss in (2), we obtain

ℒ⁡(ℳ,f,c,d)=∫𝒳f⁡(x)​min​{c⁡(x),ϕ⁡(d⁡(x,ℳ))}​𝑑x\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M};f,c,d)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(x)\min\{c(x),\phi(d(x,\mathcal{M}))\}\,dx
=∑q∈Qp⁡(q)​min​{c⁡(q),ϕ⁡(d⁡(q,ℳ))}\displaystyle=\sum_{q\in Q}p(q)\min\{c(q),\phi(d(q,\mathcal{M}))\}

Thus, on this restricted class of instances, the continuous semantic caching problem reduces exactly to the discrete semantic caching problem of (Liu et al., 2026). Therefore, if we could solve the continuous problem in polynomial time, then we could also solve the discrete problem in polynomial time. Since the latter is NP-hard, the continuous semantic caching problem is also NP-hard. ∎

Proof of Lemma 5.2.

We allocate a failure probability of δ/2\delta/2 to each of the three events to satisfy a global union bound.

1. Arrival Concentration (ℰarr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{arr}}):
Following the exact derivation using Hoeffding’s inequality and the 2m2^{m} subsets from the proof of Lemma 4.2, for a fixed round tt and an ϵ\epsilon-net of size up to meffm_{\text{eff}}, the variation distance satisfies ℙ(∥𝒘^t−𝒘∥1≥ϵb)≤2meffexp(−tϵb2/2)\mathbb{P}(\|\hat{\bm{w}}_{t}-\bm{w}\|_{1}\geq\epsilon_{b})\leq 2^{m_{\text{eff}}}\exp(-t\epsilon_{b}^{2}/2). To ensure this holds uniformly over all t∈[T]t\in[T], we apply a union bound over TT rounds. Assigning a failure probability of δ2​T2≤δ2​T\frac{\delta}{2T^{2}}\leq\frac{\delta}{2T} to each round tt, we set 2mmaxexp(−tϵb2/2)=δ2​T22^{m_{\max}}\exp(-t\epsilon_{b}^{2}/2)=\frac{\delta}{2T^{2}}. Solving for ϵb\epsilon_{b} yields the bound in ℰarr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{arr}}, which holds with probability at least 1−δ/21-\delta/2.

2. Cost Concentration (ℰcost\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cost}}):
Instead of analyzing the fixed-sample KRR bias and noise terms as in Lemma 4.2, the online setting requires an any-time bound. This follows directly from Theorem 2 in (Chowdhury and Gopalan, 2017). Applying this result with a failure probability of δ/2\delta/2 directly yields ℰcost\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cost}}. By the union bound, the two events hold simultaneously with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Lemma A.1 (Nearest-neighbor radius from local sample count).

Let B⁡(z,υ):={x∈ℝde:‖x−z‖2≤υ}B(z,\upsilon):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}:\|x-z\|_{2}\leq\upsilon\} denote the Euclidean ball of radius υ\upsilon centered at zz. Fix a cell Vi⊂ℝdeV_{i}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} with Euclidean diameter

Di:=supx,y∈Vi‖x−y‖2.D_{i}:=\sup_{x,y\in V_{i}}\|x-y\|_{2}.

Let Oi={zi,1,…,zi,Ni}⊂ViO_{i}=\{z_{i,1},\dots,z_{i,N_{i}}\}\subset V_{i} be Ni≥1N_{i}\geq 1 i.i.d. samples drawn from a probability measure μi\mu_{i} supported on ViV_{i}. Assume there exists a constant ν¯i>0\underline{\nu}_{i}>0 such that for every z∈Viz\in V_{i} and every υ∈(0,Di]\upsilon\in(0,D_{i}] with B⁡(z,υ)∩Vi≠∅B(z,\upsilon)\cap V_{i}\neq\emptyset,

μi​(B⁡(z,υ)∩Vi)≥ν¯i​(υDi)p.\mu_{i}\big(B(z,\upsilon)\cap V_{i}\big)\;\geq\;\underline{\nu}_{i}\left(\frac{\upsilon}{D_{i}}\right)^{p}.

Let xi∈Vix_{i}\in V_{i} be the representative of the cell, and define the nearest-neighbor radius

ri:=min1≤j≤Ni⁡‖xi−zi,j‖2.r_{i}:=\min_{1\leq j\leq N_{i}}\|x_{i}-z_{i,j}\|_{2}.

Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

ri≤Di​(log⁡(1/δ)ν¯i​Ni)1/p.r_{i}\;\leq\;D_{i}\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\underline{\nu}_{i}N_{i}}\right)^{1/p}.
Proof.

Fix υ∈(0,Di]\upsilon\in(0,D_{i}]. By the lower-mass assumption applied at the point xix_{i},

μi​(B⁡(xi,υ)∩Vi)≥ν¯i​(υDi)p.\mu_{i}\big(B(x_{i},\upsilon)\cap V_{i}\big)\;\geq\;\underline{\nu}_{i}\left(\frac{\upsilon}{D_{i}}\right)^{p}.

The event {ri>υ}\{r_{i}>\upsilon\} is exactly the event that none of the NiN_{i} i.i.d. samples falls in B⁡(xi,υ)∩ViB(x_{i},\upsilon)\cap V_{i}. Hence

ℙ⁡(ri>υ)=(1−μi​(B⁡(xi,υ)∩Vi))Ni\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(r_{i}>\upsilon)=\left(1-\mu_{i}(B(x_{i},\upsilon)\cap V_{i})\right)^{N_{i}}
≤exp⁡(−Ni​μi​(B⁡(xi,υ)∩Vi)),\displaystyle\leq\exp\!\left(-N_{i}\,\mu_{i}(B(x_{i},\upsilon)\cap V_{i})\right),

where we used 1−u≤e−u1-u\leq e^{-u} for u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]. Therefore,

ℙ⁡(ri>υ)≤exp⁡(−ν¯i​Ni​(υDi)p).\mathbb{P}(r_{i}>\upsilon)\leq\exp\!\left(-\underline{\nu}_{i}N_{i}\left(\frac{\upsilon}{D_{i}}\right)^{p}\right).

Now choose

υ=Di​(log⁡(1/δ)ν¯i​Ni)1/p.\upsilon=D_{i}\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\underline{\nu}_{i}N_{i}}\right)^{1/p}.

Then

ℙ⁡(ri>υ)≤δ,\mathbb{P}(r_{i}>\upsilon)\leq\delta,

which proves the claim. ∎

Remark 1.

The lower-mass condition is a standard regularity assumption in non-parametric estimation and nearest-neighbor analysis. In the specific setting of semantic caching for LLM serving, user queries are mapped into a high-dimensional embedding space ℝde\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}, but the actual data distribution concentrates on a much lower-dimensional manifold dictated by semantic similarity. This assumption is reasonable here as it simply states that within any localized semantic neighborhood (a cell ViV_{i}), the distribution of user queries is dense and well-behaved. It ensures that the probability of encountering a prompt within a radius ν\nu scales consistently with the intrinsic dimenion pp of that semantic cluster, reflecting the natural clustering tendencies of real-world text embeddings.

Lemma A.2 (Geometry-based upper bound on the KRR width).

Let κ\kappa be the unit-variance RBF kernel

κ⁡(x,x′)=exp⁡(−‖x−x′‖222​ℓk2),\kappa(x,x^{\prime})=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\ell_{k}^{2}}\right),

and let O={z1,…,zℓ}O=\{z_{1},\dots,z_{\ell}\} be the set of inputs on which the serving cost is observed. For a fixed representative xi∈𝒮x_{i}\in\mathcal{S}, let

Oi:=O∩Vi,ri:=minz∈Oi⁡‖xi−z‖2,O_{i}:=O\cap V_{i},\qquad r_{i}:=\min_{z\in O_{i}}\|x_{i}-z\|_{2},

with the convention ri=∞r_{i}=\infty if Oi=∅O_{i}=\emptyset. Then, whenever Oi≠∅O_{i}\neq\emptyset,

σℓ,λ​(xi)≤(1−e−ri2/(2ℓk2))≤min⁡{2,2ℓk​ri}.\sigma_{\ell,\lambda}(x_{i})\leq\sqrt{2\!\left(1-e^{-r_{i}^{2}/(2\ell_{k}^{2})}\right)}\leq\min\left\{\sqrt{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\ell_{k}}r_{i}\right\}.
Proof.

Let zi⋆∈Oiz_{i}^{\star}\in O_{i} attain the minimum in the definition of rir_{i}. The posterior width σℓ,λ​(xi)\sigma_{\ell,\lambda}(x_{i}) is the RKHS norm of the residual after projecting κ⁡(xi,⋅)\kappa(x_{i},\cdot) onto the span of the observed kernel atoms. Projecting onto a larger span can only decrease the residual norm, hence

σℓ,λ​(xi)≤‖κ⁡(xi,⋅)−Πspan⁡{κ⁡(zi⋆,⋅)}​κ​(xi,⋅)‖ℋ.\sigma_{\ell,\lambda}(x_{i})\leq\bigl\|\kappa(x_{i},\cdot)-\Pi_{\mathrm{span}\{\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},\cdot)\}}\kappa(x_{i},\cdot)\bigr\|_{\mathcal{H}}.

Since the orthogonal projection error onto any subspace is bounded by the error of any particular element in that subspace, and κ⁡(zi⋆,⋅)∈span⁡{κ⁡(zi⋆,⋅)}\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},\cdot)\in\mathrm{span}\{\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},\cdot)\}, we further have

‖κ⁡(xi,⋅)−Πspan⁡{κ⁡(zi⋆,⋅)}​κ​(xi,⋅)‖ℋ≤‖κ⁡(xi,⋅)−κ⁡(zi⋆,⋅)‖ℋ.\bigl\|\kappa(x_{i},\cdot)-\Pi_{\mathrm{span}\{\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},\cdot)\}}\kappa(x_{i},\cdot)\bigr\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\kappa(x_{i},\cdot)-\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}}.

For the RBF kernel,

‖κ⁡(xi,⋅)−κ⁡(zi⋆,⋅)‖ℋ2\displaystyle\|\kappa(x_{i},\cdot)-\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},\cdot)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} =κ⁡(xi,xi)+κ⁡(zi⋆,zi⋆)−2​κ​(xi,zi⋆)\displaystyle=\kappa(x_{i},x_{i})+\kappa(z_{i}^{\star},z_{i}^{\star})-2\kappa(x_{i},z_{i}^{\star})
=2​(1−exp⁡(−‖xi−zi⋆‖222​ℓk2))\displaystyle=2\left(1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x_{i}-z_{i}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\ell_{k}^{2}}\right)\right)
=2​(1−exp⁡(−ri22​ℓk2)).\displaystyle=2\left(1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{r_{i}^{2}}{2\ell_{k}^{2}}\right)\right).

Taking square roots gives the first inequality. For the second inequality, use

1−e−u≤min⁡{1,u},u≥0.1-e^{-u}\leq\min\{1,u\},\qquad u\geq 0.

Substituting u=ri2/(2​ℓk2)u=r_{i}^{2}/(2\ell_{k}^{2}) yields

2(1−e−ri2/(2ℓk2))≤min⁡{2,2ℓk​ri}.∎\sqrt{2\left(1-e^{-r_{i}^{2}/(2\ell_{k}^{2})}\right)}\leq\min\left\{\sqrt{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\ell_{k}}r_{i}\right\}.\qed

Under the assumptions of Lemmas A.1 and A.2, for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

σℓ,λ​(xi)≤min⁡{2,2​Diℓk​(log⁡(1/δ)ν¯i​Ni)1/p}.\sigma_{\ell,\lambda}(x_{i})\leq\min\left\{\sqrt{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}D_{i}}{\ell_{k}}\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\underline{\nu}_{i}N_{i}}\right)^{1/p}\right\}.

Remark 2.

To determine the optimal value of the discretization radius ϵ∗\epsilon^{*}, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the suboptimality gap bound derived in the offline setting. First we substitute the covering number relation m=𝒪⁡(ϵ−de)m=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-d_{e}}) into the three main error terms of the bound. If we assume the data distribution is relatively uniform across the paritions such that νi=O⁡(1/m)\nu_{i}=O(1/m), it follows that ∑i=1mνi−1=𝒪⁡(m2)\sum_{i=1}^{m}\nu_{i}^{-1}=\mathcal{O}(m^{2}). The term due to discretization error scales linearly with ϵ\epsilon so it is 𝒪⁡(ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon). The generalization gap term arising from the weight concentration scales as 𝒪(m/n)=𝒪(ϵ−de/2n−1/2)\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{m/n}\right)=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-d_{e}/2}n^{-1/2}) and the cost estimation gap arising from the estimation of the cost function within partitions scales as 𝒪(ϵ⋅n−1/p⋅m2/p)=𝒪(ϵ1/2−de/p⋅n−1/(2p))\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\epsilon\cdot n^{-1/p}\cdot m^{2/p}}\right)=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{1/2-d_{e}/p}\cdot n^{-1/(2p)}).

To minimize the overall bound, we must balance the growing terms with the shrinking terms with ϵ\epsilon. Due to the exponents of de/2d_{e}/2 and de/p−1/2d_{e}/p-1/2, there is a phase transition governed by the relationship between the embedding dimension ded_{e} and the intrinsic dimension pp. The generalization gap dominates when de/2≥de/p−1/2d_{e}/2\geq d_{e}/p-1/2, which simplifies to p≥2​dede+1p\geq\frac{2d_{e}}{d_{e}+1}. For case 1 when p≥de−2p\geq d_{e}-2, the generalization gap acts as the main bottleneck and we find the optimal ϵ∗\epsilon^{*} by balancing the discretization gap with the generalization gap:

By the definition of an ϵ\epsilon-net over a compact metric space 𝒳\mathcal{X} with diameter DD and intrinsic dimension pp, the maximum number of ϵ\epsilon-balls required to cover the space is strictly finite. A.2. CLCB-Frozen-Cont algorithm

The CLCB-Frozen-Cont algorithm is designed to optimize continuous semantic caching by operating in discrete, stable stages to balance learning query costs with exploiting the cache. Algorithm 6 processes incoming queries and relies on Algorithm 8 to track empriical query frequencies against a fixed frozen candidate pool. This subroutine maps incoming queries to their nearest neighbors within a membership radius (ρ)(\rho) (Algorithm 8, lines 2-6) and computes confidence bounds on these weights. It triggers a cache update (SWITCH) only when the uncertainty of the empirical estimates falls below exponentially decaying stage tolerances (Algorithm 8, lines 15-16), which limits the number of updates. Here βt=B+R​2​(γt+ln⁡(1/δt))\beta_{t}=B+R\sqrt{2(\gamma_{t}+\ln(1/\delta_{t}))} and γt:=12​log​det(I+Kt/λ)\gamma_{t}:=\frac{1}{2}\log\det\!\big(I+K_{t}/\lambda\big) is the standard information gain. When a switch occurs, the algorithm updates the frozen pool and determines the new optimal cache subset of size kk. It does this by utilizing KRR to estimate the LCB of the costs and feeding those into Cont_Reverse_Greedy. Finally for the actual routing of each query Algorithm 7 makes an optimistic online decision: it queries the LLM if the LCB of the cost is lower than the mismatch penalty of utilizing the nearest cached item, otherwise, it serves the response directly from the cache.

A.2.1. Theoretical Guarantees for CLCB-Frozen-Cont

Assumption 3 (Random Cover).

Let U¯s\bar{U}_{s} denote a frozen pool of nstotaln_{s}^{\text{total}} unique queries drawn i.i.d from ff. By standard ϵ−\epsilon-net arguments for metric spaces, there exists a universal constant Cc​o​v>0C_{cov}>0 such that, with high probability, the outlier probability mass p⊥,s−p_{\bot,s}-defined as the probability of drawing a query outside the union of balls of radius ρ\rho centered at the points in U¯s−\bar{U}_{s}-is bounded by:

p⊥,s≤𝒪~​(Cc​o​v​(1/ρ)pnstotal)\displaystyle p_{\bot,s}\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(C_{cov}\frac{(1/\rho)^{p}}{n_{s}^{\text{total}}}\right)
Lemma A.5 (Tolerance-Bounded Quantization Error).

Let ℒ⁡(ℳ)=𝔼x∼f​[gℳ​(x)]\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim f}[g_{\mathcal{M}}(x)] denote the true expected continuous loss where and let ℒs​(ℳ)=𝔼z∼ws∗​[gℳ​(z)]\mathcal{L}_{s}(\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim w_{s}^{*}}[g_{\mathcal{M}}(z)] denote the empirical proxy loss evaluated over the frozen pool U¯s\bar{U}_{s}, where the loss function gg is Lg−L_{g}-Lipschitz as established before and bounded by 1. Assume the algorithm defines a dynamic membership radius parameterized by the stage tolerance es>0e_{s}>0:

ρs≜es2​Lg\displaystyle\rho_{s}\triangleq\frac{e_{s}}{2L_{g}}

Furthermore, assume that at the beginning of stage ss, the total number of unique historical queries nstotal=|U¯s|n_{s}^{\text{total}}=|\bar{U}_{s}| satisfies the following lower bound:

nstotal≥𝒪~​(2​Cc​o​v​(2​Lg)pesp+1)\displaystyle n_{s}^{\text{total}}\geq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{2C_{cov}(2L_{g})^{p}}{e_{s}^{p+1}}\right)

Then, with high probability, the quantization bias for any cache ℳ\mathcal{M} is strictly upper bounded by the stage tolerance:

supℳ|ℒ⁡(ℳ)−ℒs​(ℳ)|≤es\displaystyle\sup_{\mathcal{M}}|\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M})-\mathcal{L}_{s}(\mathcal{M})|\leq e_{s}
Proof.

We begin by establishing a uniform upper bound on the quantization bias. By definition, the deviation between the continuous expected loss and the empirical proxy loss can be bounded by moving the absolute value inside the expectation:

|ℒ​(ℳ)−ℒs​(ℳ)|\displaystyle|\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M})-\mathcal{L}_{s}(\mathcal{M})| =|𝔼x∼f​[ℓ⁡(x,ℳ)]−𝔼z∼ws⋆​[ℓ⁡(z,ℳ)]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{x\sim f}[\ell(x;\mathcal{M})]-\mathbb{E}_{z\sim w_{s}^{\star}}[\ell(z;\mathcal{M})]\right|
≤𝔼x∼f​[|ℓ⁡(x,ℳ)−ℓ⁡(z⁡(x),ℳ)|]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim f}\left[|\ell(x;\mathcal{M})-\ell(z(x);\mathcal{M})|\right]

By applying the Law of Total Expectation, we partition the integration space into an anchored region where the queries are mapped to a nearest neighbor within ρs\rho_{s}, bounded by the Lg−L_{g}-Lipschitz property and an outlier region where the queries are unmapped, denoted by ⊥\bot and bounded by 1. Taking the supremum over all caches ℳ\mathcal{M} yields:

(12) supℳ|ℒ⁡(ℳ)−Ls​(ℳ)|≤Lg​ρs⋅(1−p⊥,s)+1⋅p⊥,s≤Lg​ρs+p⊥,s\sup_{\mathcal{M}}|\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{M})-L_{s}(\mathcal{M})|\leq L_{g}\rho_{s}\cdot(1-p_{\bot,s})+1\cdot p_{\bot,s}\leq L_{g}\rho_{s}+p_{\bot,s}

Now we bound each of these two additive terms by es/2e_{s}/2.

By the definition of our dynamic radius schedule, we substitute ρs=es2​Lg\rho_{s}=\frac{e_{s}}{2L_{g}} directly into the anchored error term, yielding:

Lg​ρs=Lg​(es2​Lg)=es2\displaystyle L_{g}\rho_{s}=L_{g}\left(\frac{e_{s}}{2L_{g}}\right)=\frac{e_{s}}{2}

To bound the outlier error term, using Assumption 3, the outlier probability p⊥,sp_{\bot,s} for the frozen pool U¯s\bar{U}_{s} evaluated at the scheduled radius ρs\rho_{s} is given by:

p⊥,s≤𝒪~​(Cc​o​v​(1/ρ)pnstotal)=𝒪~​(Cc​o​v​(2​Lg/es)pnstotal)\displaystyle p_{\bot,s}\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(C_{cov}\frac{(1/\rho)^{p}}{n_{s}^{\text{total}}}\right)=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(C_{cov}\frac{(2L_{g}/e_{s})^{p}}{n_{s}^{\text{total}}}\right)

To ensure this error satisfies p⊥,s≤es2,p_{\bot,s}\leq\frac{e_{s}}{2}, we impose the following inequality:

𝒪~​(Cc​o​v​(2​Lg/es)pnstotal)≤es2\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(C_{cov}\frac{(2L_{g}/e_{s})^{p}}{n_{s}^{\text{total}}}\right)\leq\frac{e_{s}}{2}

Rearranging this inequality to solve for the threshold of the pool size nstotal,n_{s}^{\text{total}}, we obtain:

nstotal≥𝒪~​(2​Cc​o​v​(2​Lg)pesp+1)\displaystyle n_{s}^{\text{total}}\geq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{2C_{cov}(2L_{g})^{p}}{e_{s}^{p+1}}\right)

By the premise of the lemma, nstotaln_{s}^{\text{total}} explicitly satisfies this threshold at the start of stage ss. Hence, the condition p⊥,s≤es2p_{\bot,s}\leq\frac{e_{s}}{2} holds with high probability. Therefore

Lg​ρs+p⊥,s≤es\displaystyle L_{g}\rho_{s}+p_{\bot,s}\leq e_{s}

∎

Lemma A.6 (Low-Switching from Decaying Uncertainty).

Let the stage tolerance be defined by the schedule es=2−2se_{s}=2^{-2^{s}} for s≥1s\geq 1. A stage ss ends at the first time step tt such that the joint uncertainty envelope satisfies Ut≤esU_{t}\leq e_{s}, where Ut=max⁡{Ut(p),Ut(c)}U_{t}=\max\{U_{t}^{(p)},U_{t}^{(c)}\}. Assume the algorithm’s pool and continuous uncertainties satisfy the following upper bounds for some constant j≥1j\geq 1:

Ut(p)≤Cp​log⁡Tt−ts+1,andUt(c)≤Cc​(log⁡T)jt\displaystyle U_{t}^{(p)}\leq C_{p}\sqrt{\frac{\log T}{t-t_{s}+1}},\quad\text{and}\quad U_{t}^{(c)}\leq C_{c}\frac{(\log T)^{j}}{\sqrt{t}}

where tst_{s} is the start time of stage ss. Then the total number of stage switches up to time TT, denoted S⁡(T)S(T), is bounded by 𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log\log T).

Proof.

For the algorithm to trigger a switch and end stage ss, the joint uncertainty must satisfy Ut≤esU_{t}\leq e_{s}. Because Ut=max⁡{Ut(p),Ut(c)}U_{t}=\max\{U_{t}^{(p)},U_{t}^{(c)}\}, this strict threshold requires both conditions to hold simultaneously:

Ut(p)≤esandUt(c)≤es\displaystyle U_{t}^{(p)}\leq e_{s}\quad\text{and}\quad U_{t}^{(c)}\leq e_{s}

Let nsn_{s} denote the total number of rounds spent in stage ss. The uncertainty condition requires that Cp​log⁡Tt−ts+1≤esC_{p}\sqrt{\frac{\log T}{t-t_{s}+1}}\leq e_{s}. Since t−ts+1t-t_{s}+1 measures the time elapsed within the current stage, this implies the stage cannot end until at least:

ns≥Cp2​log⁡Tes2\displaystyle n_{s}\geq\frac{C_{p}^{2}\log T}{e_{s}^{2}}

While the continuous uncertainty Ut(c)U_{t}^{(c)} may require the absolute time tt to be large, the stage duration nsn_{s} is strictly lower-bounded by the time required for the pool uncertainty to decay. If Ut(c)U_{t}^{(c)} decays slower than Ut(p)U_{t}^{(p)}, it only forces the stage to last longer, which would further decrease the total number of switches. Therefore, taking the minimum required duration is a valid conservative bound.

Substituting the tolerance schedule es=2−2se_{s}=2^{-2^{s}}, we get es2=2−2s+1e_{s}^{2}=2^{-2^{s+1}}, yields the lower bound:

ns≥Cp2​(log⁡T)​22s+1\displaystyle n_{s}\geq C_{p}^{2}(\log T)2^{2^{s+1}}

Let SS be the total number of stages initiated up to time TT. The total time horizon TT is the sum of the lengths of all completed stages, plus the final incomplete stage. Therefore, TT is strictly lower bounded by the duration of the second-to-last stage, nS−1n_{S-1}:

T=∑s=1Sns≥nS−1≥Cp2​(log⁡T)​22S\displaystyle T=\sum_{s=1}^{S}n_{s}\geq n_{S-1}\geq C_{p}^{2}(\log T)2^{2^{S}}

Rearranging to isolate SS:

22S≤TCp2​log⁡T≤T\displaystyle 2^{2^{S}}\leq\frac{T}{C_{p}^{2}\log T}\leq T

Taking the logarithm of both sides yields 2S≤log2⁡T2^{S}\leq\log_{2}T. Taking the logarithm a second time gives:

S≤log2⁡log2​T\displaystyle S\leq\log_{2}\log_{2}T

Hence, the total number of switches by time TT is bounded by 𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log\log T). ∎

Theorem A.7 (Regret Bound for CLCB-Frozen-Cont).

Suppose the algorithm is run for TT rounds with a cache size kk and a maximum item cost cmax≤1c_{\max}\leq 1. Let the stage tolerance follow the schedule es=2−2se_{s}=2^{-2^{s}}. Assume the pool uncertainty decays as Ut(p)=𝒪⁡((log⁡T)/n)U_{t}^{(p)}=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{(\log T)/n}) where nn is the time elapsed in the current stage, and the continuous cost function satisfies a kernel growth condition with information gain γt≤Cγ​(log⁡(1+t/λ))j\gamma_{t}\leq C_{\gamma}(\log(1+t/\lambda))^{j} for some j≥1j\geq 1. Then, with high probability, the cumulative α\alpha-regret of the algorithm according to the definition in section 5.1 is:

(StageBound) Ut(c)≤es,Ut(p)≤es⇒Ut≤esU_{t}^{(c)}\leq e_{s},\quad U_{t}^{(p)}\leq e_{s}\quad\Rightarrow\quad U_{t}\leq e_{s}

where Ut≜max⁡{Ut(p),Ut(c)}U_{t}\triangleq\max\{U_{t}^{(p)},U_{t}^{(c)}\}.
